did_you_know.text: The Hebrew root ש־ב־ת means “to stop” or “cease,” not merely to rest from tiredness. The verse therefore describes the ending of creative work.
The Hebrew word toledot can mean “generations,” but also an account or record of what follows. In Genesis, it appears several times as a heading for major sections.
The verse plays on the Hebrew similarity between adam, “human,” and adamah, “ground.” This wordplay highlights humanity’s connection to the physical earth.

The Hiddekel is generally identified with the Tigris, and the Perat with the Euphrates, both known today. The identities of the Pishon and Gihon are uncertain, so the exact location of Eden remains debated.
The verbs “to work” and “to guard” can also mean “to serve” and “to keep.” Humanity is presented not only as enjoying the garden, but also as responsible for it.

The word ezer does not necessarily mean an inferior assistant; elsewhere in the Bible, God himself is called an ezer, or helper. Kenegdo suggests someone corresponding to, facing, or standing alongside him.

The word tsela is usually translated as “rib,” but elsewhere in the Bible it often means a side or flank, such as the side of a structure. This is why scholars debate whether the verse means a rib or a side of the human.

The verse creates a wordplay between ish, “man,” and ishah, “woman,” a connection that is clear in Hebrew but mostly lost in English. It shows how the Bible uses the sound of words to emphasize an idea.
